rows.gloss: showering the essence of illumined things

items.question: How are the sun and moon principles defined in this doctrine of light?
premises: Mere light that is clearly manifest is called the sun.
That which distinctly showers the essence of illumined things is called the moon.
items.inference: The sun represents pure manifest light, while the moon represents the reflective disclosure of illumined objects.
items.plain_english: What is clearly manifest as sheer light is called the sun. What distinctly pours forth the essential aspects of things that are illumined is called the moon.

rows.gloss: they call the means of knowing

items.question: How do the sun and moon relate as knowing and knowable while remaining independent?
premises: The sun is called the means of knowing and the moon the knowable.
These two are not separated from each other.
Both also stand as independent.
items.inference: Knowing and knowable are inseparable in function yet each retains its own independence.
items.plain_english: They call the sun the means of knowing and the moon the knowable. Though inseparable from each other, both of them also stand as independent.

rows.gloss: this, having the nature of both enjoyer and enjoyed, turned toward each other
having the form of blazing consciousness

items.question: What arises when the enjoyer and the enjoyed turn toward each other?
premises: The same reality has the nature of both enjoyer and enjoyed.
It becomes mutually turned toward itself.
In that state it takes the form of blazing consciousness.
items.inference: The mutual facing of enjoyer and enjoyed is proclaimed as fire, the blazing form of consciousness.
items.plain_english: When this reality, which is both enjoyer and enjoyed, turns toward itself, it becomes blazing consciousness and is proclaimed as fire.

rows.gloss: not dependent because of identity with the knowable

items.question: What is the supreme principle of fire in relation to the knower and consciousness?
premises: The supreme principle of fire is this very reality of the knower.
That reality is consciousness alone.
Because it is identical with the knowable, it does not depend on anything else.
items.inference: The highest fire is the knower's own consciousness, self-sufficient through its identity with the knowable.
items.plain_english: The supreme principle of fire is nothing other than the knower's own reality. It is consciousness alone, and because it is one with the knowable, it depends on nothing outside itself.

rows.gloss: called the knower because of independence
because of differences in the knowable
expanded by the shining of variety arising from burnable things in the moon aspect

items.question: Why is consciousness called the knower and why does it appear varied?
premises: Consciousness is called the knower because of its independence.
It appears varied because of differences in the knowable.
That variety is expanded by the shining of diversity arising from burnable objects in the moon aspect.
items.inference: The one independent knower appears manifold through the differentiated objects reflected in its moon aspect.
items.plain_english: Because it is independent, consciousness is called the knower. It appears varied through differences in the knowable, and that variety is amplified by the shining of diverse objects that arise in its moon aspect.

rows.gloss: thus fire was declared as the many-rayed one by the great lord
entirely independent of the whole set of means beginning with the knowable

items.question: Why is consciousness described as fire independent of the means of knowledge?
premises: The great lord declared fire as the many-rayed one.
The state of consciousness is entirely independent of the whole set of means beginning with the knowable.
items.inference: Consciousness is called fire because it shines by itself, without relying on the apparatus of knowing.
items.plain_english: For this reason the great lord called fire the many-rayed one. The state of consciousness does not depend on the knowable or on any other means of knowledge.

rows.gloss: the abiding state is I am the knower
as by one who knows scripture
having the nature of known experience

items.question: Why is the one who says I am the knower not truly a knower in essence?
premises: The abiding state is expressed as I am the knower.
Such a one is known like a person who knows scripture.
That state has the nature of known experience, not of the knower's essential form.
items.inference: The reflective sense of being a knower is an objectified experience, not the knower's true nature.
items.plain_english: When one stands in the state of saying, I am the knower, that is known in the way a scholar knows something. It is not the knower in essence, because it has the character of an experienced object.

rows.gloss: it depends on a pure knowable and so on

items.question: When is knowership properly attributed if it depends on a knowable?
premises: True knowership is not that which depends on a pure knowable and so on.
In such a dependent state, knowership is still spoken of.
It is spoken of only by force of fitness or suitability.
items.inference: Dependent knowership is a conventional attribution, not the ultimate nature of the knower.
items.plain_english: Knowership is not truly that state in which one depends on a pure knowable and other such factors. In that condition it is called knowership only in a secondary sense, because of suitability.

rows.gloss: because of the absence of temporal sequence

items.question: How can consciousness surge forth without being divided by temporal sequence?
premises: That measuring function is constructed by a prior knower.
Consciousness may surge forth.
It does so without temporal sequence.
items.inference: The sequencing belongs to constructed cognition, while consciousness itself surges forth beyond time.
items.plain_english: That act of measuring is something set up by a prior knower. Consciousness itself may surge forth, but it does so without being divided into temporal sequence.

rows.gloss: having the form of knower, knowable, and so on
fit for sequence because of division by time

items.question: What distinguishes the fullness of consciousness from sequential action?
premises: Consciousness, once arisen, is already full.
It contains the forms of knower, knowable, and the rest.
Actions like cooking are suited to sequence because they are divided by time.
items.inference: Consciousness is intrinsically complete, whereas ordinary actions unfold through temporal division.
items.plain_english: Consciousness, as soon as it arises, is already full and includes the knower, the knowable, and the rest. Actions such as cooking, by contrast, unfold in sequence because they are divided by time.

rows.gloss: even if barren in the final moment as conceived
the state of being moon, sun, and fire

items.question: How does the example of cooking clarify the triadic nature of the light principle?
premises: A process conceived as barren in its final moment does not attain the completed state of being cooked.
The principle of light is established as moon, sun, and fire.
items.inference: Unlike time-bound processes, the light principle is established as a complete triadic reality.
items.plain_english: Something that is thought to be empty in its final moment does not truly reach the state of being cooked. In this way, the principle of light is established as having the nature of moon, sun, and fire.

rows.gloss: that state of being mere light

items.question: Does the triadic differentiation remove the primary nature of mere light?
premises: The primary nature of these is mere light.
That primary nature is not excluded.
Their first, short form is called the sun.
items.inference: Even in differentiation, the triad remains grounded in mere light, first appearing as the short solar form.
items.plain_english: Even so, their primary nature as sheer light is not set aside. The first, short form among them is called the sun.

rows.gloss: through long resting by the force of stirring and bliss
beyond the bliss of the moon

items.question: How are the moon and the prolonged state distinguished within the unfolding of light?
premises: Through stirring and bliss there is a long resting, and this is called the moon.
Beyond that there is a supreme prolonged state.
That prolonged state stands beyond the bliss of the moon.
items.inference: The lunar phase is a blissful resting, while the prolonged phase transcends even lunar bliss.
items.plain_english: Through the force of stirring and bliss there arises a long resting, and that is called the moon. Beyond it stands a supreme prolonged state, higher even than the bliss of the moon.

items.question: What do the experts call the fiery form when the three abodes are established?
premises: Experts in scripture call that light-form fiery.
Here mere light remains present when the triad of abodes is established.
items.inference: The fiery designation names mere light as it abides through the threefold structure.
items.plain_english: Those skilled in scripture call that luminous form fiery. Here, when the three abodes are established, what remains is sheer light.

rows.gloss: bearing only its reflection, as for example

items.question: How is the Shiva-point related to the letter ma in scriptural teaching?
premises: In scripture this is spoken of as the point.
That point is regarded as the Shiva-point.
It is other than the letter ma and bears only its reflection.
items.inference: The Shiva-point is distinct from the phoneme ma, though ma reflects it.
items.plain_english: In the scriptures this is described as the point and is regarded as the Shiva-point. It is different from the letter ma, bearing only a reflection of it.

rows.gloss: established in the forms of ṣa, ṭha, and visarga
another by the reflection of a portion of the letter ra

items.question: How do phonemic reflections illustrate the relation between underlying and derived forms?
premises: The letters ra, la, and ha are established in the forms of ṣa, ṭha, and visarga.
Another vowel arises as i through the reflection of a portion of ra.
items.inference: Phonemic forms can arise as reflections or transformations of prior sonic elements.
uncertainties: The exact phonetic mapping is compressed and follows traditional tantric phonology.
items.plain_english: Just as ra, la, and ha are established in the forms of ṣa, ṭha, and visarga, so another vowel appears as i through the reflected trace of ra.

rows.gloss: even though a vowel in two ways

items.question: What is the supreme inner impulse that arises from the great lord?
premises: From the great lord arises another principle, even if described as a twofold vowel.
Within it there is an inner desire to emit.
That desire is declared to be the supreme Kaula power.
items.inference: The supreme Kaula power is the lord's inner impulse toward emanation.
uncertainties: The phrase dvedhāsvaraḥ is doctrinally compressed and may refer to a specific phonemic teaching.
items.plain_english: In the same way, from the great lord arises another principle, even if spoken of as a twofold vowel. Its inner desire to emit is declared to be the supreme Kaula power.

rows.gloss: by the force of stirring becomes
in the discussion ending with the pervasion of the kalas

items.question: How does the supreme Kaula power become the power of emission?
premises: That same supreme power, by the force of stirring, becomes emission.
This is stated in the Trishiras scripture.
It is stated in the discussion that culminates in the pervasion of the kalas.
items.inference: The stirring of the supreme Kaula power manifests as visarga, the act of emanative emission.
items.plain_english: That same power, stirred into motion, certainly becomes the power of emission. This is taught in the Trishiras scripture in the section dealing with the pervasion of the kalas.

rows.gloss: therefore having the form of nectar
by the movement of the point in its own higher and lower nature

items.question: What is the seventeenth phase and how does it spread?
premises: The seventeenth phase has the form of nectar.
It spreads through the movement of the point.
That movement occurs in the point's own higher and lower nature.
items.inference: The nectar-like seventeenth phase unfolds through the dynamic movement of the bindu across its levels.
items.plain_english: The seventeenth phase, whose nature is nectar, spreads out through the movement of the point in its own higher and lower forms.

items.question: How is the power described when it remains without emission?
premises: All things are what is to be illumined.
When devoid of emission, that same power is called the coiled power.
It is likewise called the coiled vital power.
items.inference: In its non-emissive state, the illuminating power abides as kundalini in both energetic and vital forms.
items.plain_english: When it is without emission, that same power, in relation to all things that are to be illumined, is called the coiled power and also the coiled vital power.

rows.gloss: at the far end of emission
is called the abode of the self of Brahman

items.question: What is the supreme power called at the farthest point of emission?
premises: At the far end of emission the power is called supreme kundalini.
It is also called the space of Shiva.
That is called the supreme abode of the self of Brahman.
items.inference: The culmination of emission is identified with supreme kundalini and the highest Shiva-space.
items.plain_english: At the farthest point of emission, that power is called the supreme kundalini. It is also called the space of Shiva and the supreme abode of the self of Brahman.

rows.gloss: the play of creation and dissolution

items.question: How are creation and dissolution understood as the lord's emissive state?
premises: The play of creation and dissolution is mere emission of the lord.
It is the casting forth of his own self within his own self.
This is the emissive state.
items.inference: Creation and dissolution are not external acts but the lord's self-emission within himself.
items.plain_english: The lord's play of creation and dissolution is nothing but emission. It is his casting forth of himself within himself, and that is the emissive state.

rows.gloss: having reached a state of contraction

items.question: What forms does emission take when it becomes contracted?
premises: Emission, once emitted, reaches a contracted state.
In that contracted state it is termed hamsa and breath.
It is also termed consonant and contact-letter.
items.inference: The same emissive power appears in contracted form as breath and as articulated phonemic elements.
items.plain_english: When emission is sent forth and then becomes contracted, it is called hamsa, breath, consonant, and also a contact-letter.

items.question: How are the supreme abode and its emissive power named in this teaching?
premises: The unsurpassed supreme abode is called akula.
The emission of that lord is called the Kaula power.
items.inference: Akula names the supreme still abode, while Kaula names its emissive power.
items.plain_english: That unsurpassed supreme abode is called akula. The emission of that lord is called the Kaula power.
